another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

apprenticeship_location.description: The country where the child has started an apprenticeship, where relevant.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Hello! I'd be happy to help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit. To assess your eligibility, I'll need to ask you a few questions.

Let's start with the basics:

**Do you have any children, and if so, how many children are you asking about?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Hi, yes I do. I'm asking about my son Alex. He's 17 and lives with me here at home.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information. So you're asking about your son Alex, who is 17 and lives with you at home.

Since Alex is 17, I need to ask: **Is Alex currently in approved education or training?**

(Approved education or training typically includes things like A-levels, Scottish Highers, NVQs up to level 3, or other similar qualifications.)

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, he's not in any approved education at the moment. He finished school but he's actually started an apprenticeship in Scotland.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information. Just to clarify:

**Is this apprenticeship in Scotland, or is it an apprenticeship in England?**

(This distinction is important for determining eligibility, as the rules differ depending on where the apprenticeship is located.)

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: It's in Scotland. We live in England, but his apprenticeship is based in Scotland.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for clarifying that. 

Just to confirm a few more details:

**Does Alex work 24 hours or more per week in this apprenticeship, and is he living with you in England while doing the apprenticeship, or has he moved to Scotland?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: He lives with me here in England. I'm not entirely sure about the exact hours - it's an apprenticeship, so I assume it's full-time, but I'd need to check the specific details if that matters.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information. The hours do matter for eligibility, so let me explain why:

According to the rules, you'll stop getting Child Benefit if your child starts paid work for 24 hours or more a week and is no longer in approved education or training. Additionally, you'll stop getting Child Benefit if your child starts an apprenticeship in England.

Since Alex's apprenticeship is in Scotland (not England), the specific rule about English apprenticeships doesn't apply. However, if he's working 24 hours or more per week and is not in approved education or training, that could affect eligibility.

**Could you check and confirm whether Alex works 24 hours or more per week in his apprenticeship?**

This will help me give you an accurate assessment of your eligibility.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Let me think... no, actually I'm pretty sure it's less than 24 hours a week. It's not a full-time arrangement - he does the apprenticeship work but it's not quite full-time hours.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for confirming that. So Alex works less than 24 hours per week in his apprenticeship in Scotland.

Just a couple more questions to complete the assessment:

1. **Do you live in the UK?**
2. **Is anyone else currently claiming Child Benefit for Alex?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, I live in the UK - we're here in England. And no, nobody else is claiming Child Benefit for Alex. It's just me - he lives with me and I'm the one looking after him.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for providing all that information. Let me just confirm one final detail:

**Is Alex receiving any benefits in his own right, such as Employment and Support Allowance or Universal Credit?**

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: No, he's not receiving any benefits in his own right. He doesn't get Universal Credit or anything like that.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Good news! **You are eligible for Child Benefit for Alex.**

Here's why:

Although Alex is 17 and not in approved education or training, you continue to qualify for Child Benefit because:

- Alex is under 20 years old
- He lives with you in the UK and you're responsible for him
- He works **less than 24 hours per week** in his apprenticeship
- His apprenticeship is in **Scotland** (the rule that stops Child Benefit only applies to apprenticeships in England)
- He's not receiving benefits in his own right (like Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance)
- Nobody else is claiming Child Benefit for him

Since none of the disqualifying conditions apply to Alex's situation, you remain eligible to claim or continue receiving Child Benefit for him.

**Please note:** If you or your partner have an individual income over £60,000, you may need to pay the High Income Child Benefit tax charge, though you would still be entitled to receive the benefit.

Is there anything else you'd like to know about Child Benefit?
